Counsel for the complainant : Sh. Kushagra Pandit. Ld. Counsel for the Accused : Sh. Ashok Chhaparia. JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, this Court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by the complainant Sh. Ashok Talwar (hereinafter referred to as "complainant") against M/s Israni Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "accused no. 1") through its Directors Sh. Vijay Israni (hereinafter referred to as "accused no. 2") and Sh. Sunny Israni (hereinafter referred to as "accused no. 3") under Section 138 AASTHA SHARMA CT Case No. 6690/2018 Ashok Talwar Vs. M/s Israni Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. Page 3 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.23 16:35:59 +0530 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 read with Section 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act "). Brief facts of the case: 2. It is the case of the complainant, A. That, the complainant had entered into a collaboration agreement with accused no. 1 on 15.12.2012 with respect to the re-development of property bearing no. A-142, Defence Colony, New Delhi-110024. That, accused no. 1 under the terms of the collaboration agreement was required to pay a certain amount to the complainant, out of which a sum of Rs. 50,00,000/- remained to be paid. That, accused persons in discharge of their legal liability, issued two cheques bearing no. 487602 and 487601 both dated 07.05.2016 in the sum of Rs. 25,00,000/- drawn on Central Bank of India, Safdarjung Enclave, New Delhi in favour of the complainant, signed by accused no. 2 and assured that the same will be honored on presentation. That, believing the assurances and representation of the accused, the complainant presented the abovesaid cheques with his banker, however the said cheques were dishonoured with the remarks "Funds Insufficient" vide return memos dated 10.05.2016 and 11.05.2016. B. In these circumstances, the complainant got issued a statutory legal demand notice to the accused through his counsel, dated 23.05.2016, thereby requiring the accused to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheques within a period of 15 days from the receipt of the said notice. The said notice under Sec. 138 of NI Act was sent to the accused through Registered AD/Speed Post/Courier at his correct address. That despite service of the above stated notice of demand, the Accused AASTHA SHARMA CT Case No. 6690/2018 Ashok Talwar Vs. M/s Israni Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. Page 4 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.23 16:36:58 +0530 has deliberately and willfully failed to comply with the said notice of demand and has failed to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within the stipulated period of 15 days from the date of receipt of the said notice. Consequently, this case was filed by the complainant against the accused, which was within the limitation period as laid down u/s 138 , NI Act. 3. In the pre-summoning evidence, the complainant examined himself on affidavit being Ex. CW1/A and relied on documents Ex. CW1/1 to Ex. CW1/9. 4. Upon prima facie consideration of the pre-summoning evidence, the accused persons were summoned. 5. Upon the appearance of the accused persons, notice under Section 251 CrPC was served upon them to which they pleaded not guilty. The accused no. 2 and 3 have admitted their signatures on the cheque in question and have stated that in 2011, two cheques of Rs. 25 lakhs were given to the complainant as security and the same were undated. The accused persons have further stated that they have made payment of Rs. 12 lakhs to Tarun Talwar, son of the complainant and Rs. 38 lakhs to the brother of the complainant who was the co-owner of the property in 2012. The accused persons have stated that total of Rs. 50 lakhs has already been paid to the complainant after which the cheques were to be returned to the accused company in the year 2012 pursuant to the delivery of the possession of the plot. The accused persons have stated that they do not owe any liability towards the complainant and that the complainant has misused the cheques in question. The accused persons have also denied receiving the legal demand notice. CT Case No. 6690/2018 Ashok Talwar Vs. M/s Israni Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. Page 5 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.23 16:37:03 +0530 6. CW-1 was examined-in-chief, cross-examined and discharged. Thereby, CE was closed on 03.10.2019. Accordingly, matter proceeded to the stage of recording the statement of the accused persons. 7. Statement of accused persons under Section 313 CrPC read with Section 281 CrPC was recorded on 05.12.2019 wherein the accused persons opted to lead defence evidence. Thereafter DE was closed vide order of this court by recording a separate statement of accused no. 3 on 04.02.2026. 8. Thereafter, the matter was listed for final arguments. After hearing the final arguments from both sides, the matter was reserved for pronouncement of judgment. 9. It is well settled position of law that to constitute an offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: I. drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, II. The cheque was issued for payment to another person for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; III. Cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. RBI in its notification DBOD.AML BC.No.47/14.01.001/2011-12 has reduced the aforesaid period from 6 months to 3 months. CT Case No. 6690/2018 Ashok Talwar Vs. M/s Israni Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. Page 6 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.05.23 16:37:07 +0530 IV. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque; V. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount; VI. Failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. The offence under Section 138 , NI Act is made out against the drawer of the cheque, only when all the aforementioned ingredients are fulfilled. 10. Analysing all the concerned provisions of law and various pronouncements in this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa [AIR 2019 SC 1983] held that: I. Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the Act mandates that a presumption be drawn that the cheque in question was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. II. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. III. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in CT Case No. 6690/2018 Ashok Talwar Vs. M/s Israni Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. Page 7 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.23 16:37:34 +0530 order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. IV. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. It is therefore implied that the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the presumptions under Section 118(a) and Section 139 have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. Appreciation of evidence and marshalling of facts: 11. Issuance of cheque: The complainant has filed on record the original cheques, i.e., bearing no. 487602 dated 07.05.2016 for Rs. 25,00,000/- and cheque bearing no. 487601 dated 07.05.2016 for Rs. 25,00,000/-, both drawn on Central Bank of India, Safdarjung Enclave, New Delhi (Ex. CW1/2 & Ex. CW1/3 respectively). In notice under Section 251 CrPC, the accused persons have admitted that the cheques in dispute belong to him. It is also not disputed that the cheques in question are not drawn on the account maintained by the accused no. 1 and it is impliedly admitted therefore that the accused no. 1 is the drawer of the cheques. Therefore, ingredient number I stands fulfilled in the present case. 12. Presentment and dishonor of cheque: As per the RBI guidelines, it is essential for the cheque in question be to presented within a period of three months CT Case No. 6690/2018 Ashok Talwar Vs. M/s Israni Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. Page 8 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.05.23 16:37:38 +0530 from the date on which they are drawn and the same be returned as unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque. In the case at hand, the cheques in question were returned vide return memos dated 10.05.2016 and 11.05.2016 (Ex. CW1/4 & Ex. CW/5 respectively) due to the reason "Funds Insufficient." By implication thereof, the cheques were presented within three months and the same were returned. Therefore, Ingredient number III & IV stand fulfilled in the present case. 13. Legal demand notice and payment by the accused thereof: The legal notice dated 23.05.2016 (Ex. CW1/6) was dispatched on 23.05.2016 vide Courier (Ex. CW1/7) (Colly.), i.e., within 30 days of return of the bank memo indicating cheques in question being unpaid. The fact that the legal demand notice has made a clear and unambiguous demand for payment of the cheque in question is not disputed. The accused persons have denied the receiving of legal demand notice in notice u/s 251 CrPC. However, as per the presumption raised under Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and Section 27 of General Clauses Act, if the legal demand notice is sent at the correct address, then the same shall be deemed to have been duly served, as per the precedent laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed , (2007) 3 SCC (Cri). The ingredient number V is fulfilled by virtue of giving of legal demand notice within 30 days from the bank return memo. The receipt of legal demand notice by the accused is deemed to be admitted as per the discussion above. CT Case No. 6690/2018 Ashok Talwar Vs. M/s Israni Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. Page 9 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.23 16:37:42 +0530 14. Moving on, it is not disputed that the accused has not made the payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal demand notice. Therefore, ingredient number VI also stands fulfilled in the present case. Presumption under Section 118A read with Section 139 , NI Act 15. The NI Act raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque, i.e., complainant; firstly, with regard to the issuance of cheque for consideration, as contained in Section 118(a) and secondly, with regard to the fact that the holder of cheque received the same for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, as contained in Section 139 of the Act. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its judgment titled Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 held that a reverse onus clause usually imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden and when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. It was further held that the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. Once a probable defence is raised, then the onus is shifted to the complainant to establish that a legally enforceable liability existed in his favour and the burden of proof on the complainant in this case is that of "beyond reasonable doubt." CT Case No. 6690/2018 Ashok Talwar Vs. M/s Israni Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. Page 10 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.23 16:37:46 +0530 16. The accused can rebut the presumption as raised under Section 138 , NI Act by: (a) putting forth his defence at the time of framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC; (b) cross-examining the complainant; (c) when statement of accused is recorded u/s 313 CrPC; (d) or by leading defence evidence, thereby demolishing the case of the complainant. Rebuttal of Presumption by Accused as to existence of legally enforceable debt 17. In light of the above discussion, since the accused has admitted to issuance of cheques, admitted the signatures on the cheques and legal notice has also been deemed to be served, what is left to be seen is whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption against him, i.e., whether the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt? 18. In the present case, in order to discharge his initial burden to prove the abovementioned ingredients, the complainant relied upon the affidavit of the complainant being Ex. CW1/A and collaboration agreement Ex. CW1/1. The case of the complainant is that the accused had issued the cheques in question in discharge of his liability of Rs. 50,00,000/- against the Clause 8 & 9 of the collaboration agreement. CT Case No. 6690/2018 Ashok Talwar Vs. M/s Israni Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. Page 11 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.23 16:37:55 +0530 19. A bare perusal of Clause 8 of the collaboration agreement reveals that an amount of Rs. 1,21,00,000/- was to be paid to the complainant by the accused builders towards consideration and out of the total consideration of Rs. 1,21,00,000/-, the accused builder has already paid a sum of Rs. 70,00,000/- to the complainant owner at the time of signing of this collaboration agreement. Further perusal of Clause 9 of the collaboration agreement reveals that balance amount of Rs. 50,00,000/- was to be paid to complainant Sh. Ashok Talwar on or before 05.04.2013, failing which interest shall have to be paid by the accused to the complainant. 20. The complainant in his cross-examination dated 03.10.2019 has admitted that his son Tarun Talwar had received Rs. 12,00,000/- in cash against receipt from the accused on 24.03.2012 towards part payment against the collaboration agreement. Receipt on record Ex. DW1/1. The complainant in his cross- examination dated 03.10.2019 has further admitted that his brother Praveen Talwar received Rs. 38,00,000/- as part payment from the accused side on 24.03.2012 against the collaboration agreement. Receipt on record Ex. DW1/2. The complainant in his cross-examination has stated that the total amount to be paid under the collaboration agreement was Rs. 1,26,00,000/- and that the builder was to pay an additional sum of Rs. 84,00,000/- to brother of the complainant Praveen Talwar. 21. It is an established rule of law that under Section 91 and 92 of Indian Evidence Act, no oral evidence can be given qua variation, subtraction, addition or contradiction of any term of any contract, grant or disposition which is reduced into a document and only documentary evidence or secondary evidence of its CT Case No. 6690/2018 Ashok Talwar Vs. M/s Israni Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. Page 12 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.05.23 16:37:59 +0530 contents are admissible. In the present case, the complainant has nowhere produced any subsequent document to contradict the collaboration agreement in question Ex. CW1/1 which states the amount to be paid as Rs. 1,21,00,000/- to the complainant, out of which Rs. 70,00,000/- has also been paid. The complainant cannot later claim that without any documentary evidence that the amount to be paid under the collaboration agreement was infact Rs. 1,26,00,000/- alongwith an additional sum of Rs. 84,00,000/- to be paid to the brother of the complainant. 22. Moreover, the complainant in her cross-examination dated 03.10.2019 has further admitted that the amount of Rs. 50,00,000/- was paid to the son and brother of the complainant on 24.03.2012, i.e., before 05.04.2013 as per the Clause 9 of the collaboration agreement. The complainant cannot seek further sum as interest or additional expense, if such term is contradictory to that mentioned in the collaboration agreement. Therefore, the complainant cannot claim that a legal enforceable liability exists for any amount more than Rs. 1,21,00,000/- as mentioned in the collaboration agreement, in absence of no subsequent agreement varying the terms of Ex. CW1/1 executed between the complainant and the accused. 23. Furthermore, the complainant has admitted in his cross-examination dated 03.10.2019 that the accused had paid Rs. 50,00,000/- to the son and the brother of the complainant as part payment against the collaboration agreement. Ld. Counsel for the complainant has argued that unless explicitly mentioned, any amount paid towards the liability is deemed to be paid towards interest and not towards principal. However, as discussed above, the Clause 9 of the collaboration agreement explicitly mentions that the interest was to be paid by the accused if the CT Case No. 6690/2018 Ashok Talwar Vs. M/s Israni Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. Page 13 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.05.23 16:38:04 +0530 remaining amount of Rs. 50,00,000/- was not paid by the accused on or before 05.04.2013. Since the complainant has himself mentioned that the amount of Rs. 50,00,000/- has been received by the accused on 24.03.2012, therefore this argument of the complainant holds no ground in light of law laid down by Section 91 and 92 of Indian Evidence Act, as discussed above. 24. In light of the same, the complainant has failed to place anything on record to indicate the liability of the accused on the date of the presentation of the cheque in question. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Dashrathbhai Trikambhai Patel v. Hitesh M. Patel (2023) 1 SCC 578 has held that "for the commission of offence u/s 138 NI Act, the cheque that is dishonoured must represent a legally enforceable debt on the date of maturity or presentation." The complainant failed to discharge the onus and no evidence was produced to show the actual liability of the accused on the date of presentation of the cheque in question. The accused persons have already rebutted their liability to the tune of the amount mentioned in the cheque in question, when the complainant admitted to receiving the sum of Rs. 50,00,000/- from the accused and the onus of proof has shifted upon the complainant to prove that the accused persons owed the liability as stated by the complainant in his cheque in question. 25. The accused persons have therefore rebutted the presumption u/s 139 NI Act by proving that the liability of the accused no. 1 is not what has been stated by the complainant in the cheque in question. While, the complainant has been unsuccessful in proving that the accused owed the liability as stated in the cheque in question, despite the payment made by the accused persons by placing on record CT Case No. 6690/2018 Ashok Talwar Vs. M/s Israni Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. Page 14 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.05.23 16:38:08 +0530 any document to indicate the liability of the accused on the date of presentation of the cheque in question. 26. In light of the discussion above, ingredient no. II has not been fulfilled in the present case. Conclusion: 27. In view of the aforesaid discussion, the accused M/s Israni Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. (accused no. 1) through its directors (accused no. 2) Sh. Vijay Israni and (accused no. 3) Sh. Sunny Israni are hereby acquitted of the offence punishable under Section 138 , Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
